ABSTRACT
Limited by process precision for silicon photonic integrated circuits (Si-PICs), manufacturing deviations in waveguide width,
etch depth, and layer thickness are inevitable. These variations cause initial phase shifts and compromise the performance
of phase-sensitive devices such as Mach-Zehnder Interferometers (MZI) and microring resonators. To address this issue, we
present a lossless, nonvolatile, and CMOS-compatible post-fabrication trimming method based on on-chip high-temperature
annealing, assisted by highly thermally isolated undercut waveguides. The significant thermal stress during annealing exceeds the
yield strength of silicon and induces microscopic modifications including irreversible lattice expansion verified by transmission
electron microscopy, which ultimately reduces the mode effective refractive index. This novel approach requires no additional
equipment beyond the standard CMOS fabrication and eliminates static power consumption after short-duration electrical
stimulus. Trimming experiments on C- and O-band MZIs demonstrated a phase compensation over 4π, a tuning resolution over 6
bits, and stable operation beyond 8500 hours. Additionally, 15 randomly MZIs are precisely trimmed to BAR, CROSS, or orthogonal
states, confirming the method’s universality. This practical technique enables reliable, scalable post-fabrication trimming for
low-cost, energy-efficient Si-PIC applications such as optical modulating, switching, and computing.
1
Introduction
Owing to high integration density, low power consumption,
low latency, and cost-effectiveness, silicon photonic integrated
circuits (Si-PICs) [1, 2] have been widely adopted in optical
communications [3–6], optical computing [7, 8], microwave
photonics [3, 9], and quantum optics [10, 11]. However, limited
by cost and fabrication precision during lithography [12, 13],
etching [14], and depositing [12], dimensional deviations in the
waveguide (WG) width, etch depth, and layer thickness inevitably
occur. Such variations induce accumulated phase errors that sig-
nificantly degrade performances of phase-sensitive devices such
as Mach-Zehnder interferometers (MZIs) [15–17] and micro-ring
resonators (MRRs) [18–21]. In MZIs, random phase differences
between interferometer arms make the initial state unpredictable
[15–17], while in MRRs, process errors shift the resonance wave-
length from its design value [18–21], compromising filtering or
selection functions. Although widening WG improves fabrication
tolerance [22–24], it also increases the device footprint [24] and
complexity of compact bending designs [22, 23], and cannot
fully eliminate phase errors. In addition, the thermo-optic effect
is commonly used for phase compensations by adjusting the
WG refractive index [15, 18, 19, 24, 25]. However, this approach
entails continuous heating power, introduces thermal manage-

ment challenges, and increases control and packaging complexity
in large-scale systems. Therefore, effective, non-volatile, and
energy-efficient post-fabrication trimming is urgently required to
ensure the reliability of Si-PICs.
Extensive research has been conducted on post-fabrication com-
pensation techniques for Si-PICs. One strategy uses femtosec-
ond (Fs) laser irradiation on the WG core surface to induce
amorphization or thinning controlled by the laser fluence [26],
ultimately altering the mode effective refractive index. Cladding
modification via Fs laser has also been demonstrated [27].
However, Fs laser modification requires dedicated laser systems,
significantly increasing cost, and introduces substantial optical
loss, degrading the Q-factor of MRRs [26] and insertion loss
of MZIs [27]. Moreover, its tuning precision remains limited.
Another approach involves germanium implantation to amor-
phize the crystalline silicon (Si) core during fabrication [28],
followed by thermal annealing to recrystallize, which reduces
the refractive index of the WG core. Nonetheless, this method
introduces additional loss and relies on non-standard custom
fabrication steps, thereby increasing cost. A third well-studied
trimming approach employs phase change materials (PCMs) [29,
30], typically chalcogenide compounds [16, 31, 32]. By applying
electrical or optical pulses within specific temperature regimes,
PCMs can reversibly switch between crystalline and amorphous
states, enabling tunable optical constants. To reduce their optical
loss and improve CMOS compatibility, strategies including wide-
bandgap PCMs [30, 31] and back-end-of-line integration [16]
have been explored. However, integrating PCMs into Si-PICs still
increases fabrication complexity and raises concerns about phase
state retention and device durability [33].
In this work, we propose a novel, lossless, and non-volatile
post-fabrication trimming method for Si-PICs based on on-chip
high-temperature annealing, enabled by the thermally isolated
undercut waveguide [19, 24, 34–37]. The annealing-induced ther-
mal stress exceeds the yield threshold of Si, leading to irreversible
material modifications and a consequent reduction in the WG’s
effective refractive index. The method is CMOS-compatible and
realized through simple electrical heating using integrated thin-
film heaters. Once trimmed, no static power is needed to maintain
the compensation effect, enabling energy-efficient operation.
This method was experimentally demonstrated on both C-band
and O-band MZI, achieving a lossless effective index reduction
of 0.0173 and phase compensation exceeding 4π in the phase-
shift waveguide (PS-WG). Additionally, it enabled at least 6-bit
optical power tuning resolution, broadband applicability, and
long-term stability over 8500 hours. Calibration of 15 randomly
MZIs further confirms the universality of this approach. This
novel technique offers a practical and groundbreaking solution
to fabrication errors, with substantial potential for improving the
reliability and scalability of Si-PICs.
2
Principle
2.1
Structure and Simulations
Figure 1a presents the schematic of a 2 × 2 MZI integrated
with undercut thermo-optic interferometer arms on a silicon-
on-insulator platform. Silica (SiO2) bridges flanking the Si WG
were adopted to enhance mechanical stability. The inset illus-
trates a detailed cross-sectional view of the undercut PS-WG.
A titanium nitride (TiN) heater is positioned above the Si WG,
with both encapsulated within SiO2 claddings. The underlying
Si substrate is selectly removed vertically and laterally to form
Si deep trenches and a suspended structure [38], which is
entirely surrounded by air with low thermal conductivity. This
design provides strong thermal isolation, leading to a signifi-
cantly greater local temperature rise per unit heating power and
improved thermo-optic efficiency (∼1.5 mW/π) compared to the
non-undercut case (∼15 mW/π).
As shown in Figure 1b, the temperature distribution along the
optical propagation direction (X-axis) was simulated using the
Lumerical 3D HEAT solver based on the structural parameters
in Table 1. The simulations were performed under an ambient
condition, with heating powers ranging from 1 to 76 mW in 5-mW
increments. Minor fluctuations in the temperature curves arise
from the bridge-like SiO2 cladding, which introduces additional
thermal leakage and lowers the local temperature relative to
the fully SiO2-free regions. At each power, the temperature
distribution peaks at the center of the PS-WG and symmetrically
decreases toward the edges due to heat leakage in non-undercut
regions. The local heating efficiency reaches 20.2 K/mW at the
center and drops to 3.2 K/mW at the boundaries. Specifically, at
heating powers of 31, 51, and 66 mW, the temperature rise of the
PS-WG center exceeds 600, 1000, and 1300 K, respectively. At the
extreme 71 mW, the center temperature reaches 1731 K, surpassing
the melting point of Si (1687 K). Besides, such undercut structures
typically exhibit sub-millisecond heating and cooling rates [39],
enabling rapid thermal response.
Figure 1c illustrates the trimming mechanism and effect through
on-chip high-temperature annealing of the undercut WG. The
thermal expansion coefficient (α) of Si (2.6 × 10−6 K−1) is
approximately five times that of SiO2 (0.5 × 10−6 K−1). During
annealing and subsequent rapid cooling of the undercut MZI,
the thermal contraction of Si is constrained by the surrounding
SiO2 layer, inducing thermal stress (σ) estimated by the equation
[40–42]:

where E is Young’s modulus of Si, Δ𝛼is the expansion coefficient
mismatch between Si and SiO2, and Δ𝑇is the temperature
change. Under low-power annealing [24, 35, 37, 39], the resulting
thermal stress remains within the elastic limit of Si, allowing it
to fully recover to the initial state upon cooling with negligible
residual stress. In contrast, at higher heating powers—especially
in undercut regions—local temperatures can easily reach 1000 ◦C.
The following rapid cooling generates substantial tensile stress
surpassing the yield strength of Si, inducing irreversible plastic
deformation in the silicon lattice, accompanied by residual tensile
stress and alterations in its band structure. Compared to pristine
silicon, the resulting lattice expansion reduces atomic density
and the interatomic orbital overlap, resulting in flattened band
curvature. These collectively weaken the electronic response to
external electric fields, thereby reducing the single-atom polariz-
ability. Notably, it is critical that the maximum temperature of the
undercut WG (at X = 0 of Figure 1b) should be below the melting
points of Si (1687K), SiO2 (1986K), and TiN (3203K) throughout

2.2
TEM Characterization
The 2 × 2 MZI chip was fabricated using the standard Multi-
Project Wafer service from Advanced Micro Foundry, with its
micrograph shown in Figure 2a. Both MZI arms employ under-
cut PS-WGs for symmetry, while only the lower arm includes
electrodes for voltage supply. Trimming was performed on the
lower arm by applying voltages of 4–10.65 V in 18 discrete steps,
corresponding to heating power of 10–76 mW, each lasting 10
s. The post-trimming phase compensation exceeding 2π was
achieved, with a detailed discussion in Section 3.1. Subsequently,
Focused Ion Beam (FIB) sampling was carried out on the central
sections of both PS-WGs for comparison, selected for their
optimal thermal isolation (Figure 2b–d). At this stage, no visible
structural differences were observed between two arms.
Later, high-resolution aberration-corrected Transmission Elec-
tron Microscopy (TEM) was used to characterize these sam-
ples (Figure 2e–h), revealing a periodic and symmetric atomic
arrangement, indicative of high crystallinity. Dumbbell-shaped
atom columns, attributed to the Si{110} family, were observed,
with each site exhibiting paired atoms. Theoretically, the spacing
between these dumbbell rows corresponds to the interplanar (d-)
spacing of the Si{111} family. The insets illustrate the enhanced
lattice images obtained through Fast Fourier Transform-based
noise filtering using Digital Micrograph software. Specifically,
Figure 2e,f shows representative TEM images from the Si WG
core and the Si–SiO2 interface of the untrimmed FIB sample. The
measured row spacing of 0.32 and 0.315 nm closely match the
theoretical d-spacing of Si(111) plane (0.314 nm) [44–46]. In con-
trast, Figure 2g,h presents representative images of the trimmed
sample, where d-spacings increase to 0.333 and 0.328 nm, respec-
tively. This confirms that high-temperature annealing followed by

3
Measurements
In detailed trimming experiments, we identified two key and
controllable parameters that significantly affect the trimming
effect: the trimming voltage Vtrim, which determines the heating
power and the resulting WG temperature, and the trimming
duration Ttrim, which sets the exposure time to elevated tem-
peratures. Using a controlled-variable approach, we conducted
multiple trimming experiments on each 2 × 2 MZI unit operating
in the C band or O band. The test setup is described in detail
in Section 6.1 of Methods. Each trimming experiment cycle
followed a consistent procedure: (1) First, a specific Vtrim was
applied for a duration Ttrim and then immediately removed; (2)
Subsequently without further electrical input, the optical fiber
was finely adjusted to optimize coupling with the chip, after
which the optical powers at two output ports of MZI (PI1−O1
and PI1−O2), were recorded. (3) Additionally, within the low
voltage regime for undercut thermo-optic structure [24, 35, 37,
39], where Si refractive index changes are reversible, the optical
transmission versus power consumption (P−T) characteristics
were also measured at both outputs after each trimming. This
sequence constituted one full trimming experiment. Either Vtrim
or Ttrim was then incrementally adjusted, and the above procedure
was repeated accordingly.
3.1
Effect of Vtrim on Trimming with a Fixed Ttrim
Trimming experiments were first performed on the C-band MZI1
with geometric parameters listed in Table 1. For each trimming,
the duration Ttrim was fixed at 10 s, while the trimming voltage
Vtrim was varied from 4 to 10.65 V across 18 discrete values,
following Steps 1–3. The recorded output optical powers PI1−O1
and PI1−O2 after removing Vtrim are summarized in Figure 3a, with
the x-axis representing Vtrim. A threshold voltage Vth between 7.9
and 8.4 V was observed, corresponding to a threshold heating
power of ∼43 mW and local temperature of ∼1100 K. More
analysis about Vth can be found in Section S2. In the first four
experiments with Vtrim (4, 5.5, 7, and 7.9 V) below Vth, PI1−O1 and
PI1−O2 remained constant, indicating no modification to the WG
refractive index. In the fifth experiment with Vtrim of 8.4 V, PI1−O1
significantly dropped by 9.5 dB, reaching near-minimum, while
PI1−O2 increased by 0.1 dB, approaching the peak power. Beyond
8.4 V, output powers at both ports varied significantly with each
trimming. Notably, a turning point was identified at 9.8 V with
a 66 mW heating power. Specifically, for Vtrim ≤9.8 V, PI1−O1
increased from its minimum to the peak, while PI1−O2 decreased
from the peak to the minimum. In contrast, when Vtrim ≥9.8 V,
PI1−O1 decreased from its peak and PI1−O2 rose from the minimum
toward a second peak. Notably, during the trimming process, the
peak of PI1−O1 (1.1 dBm at 9.8 V) was close to that of PI1−O2 (1.2 dBm
at 8.4 V). To accurately assess trimming-induced losses, the total

After each trimming, the periodic P−T responses for the I1–O1
and I1–O2 paths of MZI1 are shown in Figure 3c,d, respectively,
with the trimming sequence marked in the color bars. It should
be noted that the heating power used here is much lower than
the trimming threshold. The initial P−T characteristics prior to
trimming are extracted and plotted as solid lines in Figure 3e.
According to the thermo-optic effect [15, 19, 24], heating raises
the WG’s real refractive index. For comparison, we also simulated
P−T curves assuming a reduction in the Si real refractive index
(dashed lines in Figure 3e), whose trend closely matches that
observed in Figure 3a for Vtrim ≥8.4 V. Specifically, both the
measured (Figure 3a) and simulated (Figure 3e dash lines) PI1−O1
curves exhibit a decrease to a minimum, followed by a rise to
a peak, and then a subsequent decline. Similarly, PI1−O2 values
(blue) decrease from the near peak to the minimum and then
increase toward the next peak. The perfect consistency between
measurement and simulation suggests that high-temperature
trimming of the undercut WG reduces the real part of the Si
refractive index.
Trimming-induced reduction in Si index counteracts the thermo-
optic effect, thereby requiring higher thermal power to maintain
the same optical power and resulting in a redshift of P−T curves
in Figure 3c,d. Specifically, in Figure 3c (bar port), the original
and 18th-trimmed P−T curves are depicted as bold black and
red lines, respectively. The intermediate trimming stages exhibit
a gradual color transition from dark to light black, followed by
light to dark red. Taking the first peak (point A) of the original
curve as a reference, a continuous redshift of the peak is observed
with successive trimmings. By the 18th trimming, the peak (point
B) surpasses the second peak (point C) of the original curve,
indicating a redshift exceeding one full period. Similarly, when
using the first trough (point D) of the original curve as a reference,
a regular redshift is observed up to the 13th trimming. After the
14th trimming, the trough shifts outside the measured range;
however, the redshift of its preceding trough (point E) still reflects
the overall trend due to the curve’s periodicity. In Figure 3d (cross
port), the original and 18th-trimmed P−T curves are shown as
bold black and blue lines, respectively, with intermediate curves
transitioning from dark to light black, and then from light blue
to dark blue. Referencing the first trough (point X) of the original
curve, a gradual redshift was observed with trimming progress.
Consequently, these redshifts in P−T curves further confirm
that trimming reduces the real refractive index of Si, which
will lower the mode effective refractive index and compensate
for fabrication-induced phase deviations. In addition, the heater
resistance before trimming was 1460 Ω. After each trimming,
it first decreased and then increased, reaching 1085 Ω after the
final trimming, due to high-temperature annealing effects. More
discussion about P−T curves can be found in Section S3.

provided in Section S5; data for O-band MZIs with a 17 µm trench
spacing are available in Sections S6 and S7.
4
Discussion
4.1
High-Precision Trimming
Based on experimental results from multiple MZIs, on-chip high-
temperature trimming induces a reduction in the Si refractive
index, resulting in a redistribution of optical power between out-
put ports. To evaluate trimming precision, a controlled variable
method was employed by individually varying Vtrim and Ttrim.
Figure 5a,b shows optical transmissions at the cross port of two
MZIs after successive trimming operations. For experiments in
Figure 5a, Ttrim was fixed at 1.5 s, while Vtrim was increased from

trimming resolution can be achieved by reducing the steps of Vtrim
and Ttrim or tuning them synchronously, indicating the method’s
promise for precise phase control in PICs.
4.2
Bidirectional Trimming
Although high-temperature trimming only reduces the Si refrac-
tive index, bidirectional optical power control in a 2 × 2 MZI
can be achieved by leveraging phase cancellation between inter-
ferometer arms. As shown in the inset of Figure 5c, the MZI
incorporates symmetric undercut thermal-optic structures on
both arms. The measured initial P–T curve is shown as solid lines
in Figure 5c, while the dashed lines represent simulated responses
under refractive index reduction. According to the prior anal-
ysis, trimming arm1 shifts the optical power distribution along
the direction associated with index reduction, causing the bar-
port power to initially decrease and then increase. Subsequent
trimming of arm2, reducing the Si refractive index in the other
arm, partially compensates for the phase shift from arm1, thereby
reversing the optical power change. This predicted behavior was
experimentally confirmed, as shown in Figure 5d. The first 20
trimmings on arm1 caused a bar-port power to drop to a minimum
and then gradually increase; after the 20th trimming, the power
remained below the peak level (–6.8 dBm vs. –0.2 dBm). The
electrical stimulus was then applied to arm2, causing the power
to return toward the minimum and ultimately approach the
initial state after the 64th trimming. This experiment successfully
demonstrates the bidirectional tuning capability of the proposed
trimming method in MZIs, significantly enhancing trimming
flexibility and facilitating rapid, efficient, and high-precision
phase compensation.
4.3
Broadband-Synchronous Trimming
For the C-band MZI used in Figure 5c,d, normalized transmission
spectra (relative to a reference grating) were measured over a
60 nm wavelength range at three stages: pre-trimming, post-
20th trimming, and post-64th trimming. As shown in Figure 5e,
consistent shifts across the entire bandwidth were observed after
each trimming operation, indicating effective index tuning over
a broad wavelength range. Additionally, wide-spectrum post-
fabrication calibration results for O-band MZI are provided in
Section S6, further demonstrating the method’s applicability
across different spectral regions.
4.4
Non-Volatile Trimming

(see Section S6), the bar-port optical power accounted for 74.2%

4.5
Universal Trimming
To verify the universality of the proposed trimming method,
15 MZIs with distinct undercut thermo-optic structures and
diverse initial states were randomly selected from the wafer. By
adjusting Vtrim and Ttrim, five MZIs were tuned to each of the
BAR (Figure 6a), CROSS (Figure 6b), and quadrature (Figure 6c)
states. In each subplot, dashed and solid lines represent the
measured P–T curves before and after trimming, with tuning
power ranges maintained below the trimming threshold. Notably,
the peak transmission remains nearly unchanged after trimming,
indicating negligible additional loss. The corresponding phase
compensation via local high-temp trimming ranges from –0.23π
to –1.92π, with each value indicated in the corresponding sub-
plot. Together, these results confirm the lossless, targeted batch
tuning of this method. Furthermore, the previously described
fine-resolution and bidirectional tuning capabilities also enable
precise achievement of arbitrary target states.
Table 2 compares the proposed method with three representa-
tive post-fabrication trimming techniques. All these techniques
are nonvolatile, requiring no continuous heating power after
trimming, thereby improving energy efficiency. Femtosecond-
laser tuning requires specialized, costly equipment and shows
poor compatibility with silicon photonics. Germanium doping
and PCM trimming introduce additional steps beyond standard
foundry processes. Although a complex process, recent advances
have enabled CMOS-compatible PCM integration [47, 48], and its
bidirectional and highly localized trimming make it particularly
suitable for precise and reconfigurable photonics systems. In con-
trast, the trimming method proposed in this work is inherently
limited to unidirectional refractive index tuning and moderate
spatial locality due to deep-trench constraints; it remains highly
attractive for nearly lossless operation with a large tuning range.
Moreover, it offers full compatibility with standard foundry
processes, significantly simplifying fabrication and reducing cost.
Specifically, it is well-suited for: (1) phase trimming of MZI phase-
shifting arms to control initial output intensity and (2) phase
trimming within microrings for resonance wavelength tuning.
Future process optimizations, such as narrowing the deep-trench
width and spacing, may further enhance spatial confinement.
5
Conclusion
In this study, we present a nonvolatile, lossless, and cost-effective
post-fabrication trimming method for Si-PICs via on-chip high-
temperature annealing, enabled by an undercut thermo-optic
structure. TEM analysis reveals that high-power treatment
induces irreversible lattice expansion in the undercut Si WG,
which ultimately promotes a reduction in the Si refractive index
for fabrication compensations. To the best of our knowledge,
this is the first report of such a technique. The method is fully
compatible with standard CMOS foundry processes and requires
no additional equipment. Moreover, it operates via simple elec-
trical heating and consumes no static power after trimming,
ensuring both ease of use and high energy efficiency. Using
both C-band and O-band MZIs, we experimentally confirm an
effective refractive index reduction of 0.0173 and fine-resolution
tuning exceeding 6 bits, with broadband operation. Notably,
the trimming effect remains stable for at least 8500 hours.
Furthermore, we achieved precise, individual tuning of 15 MZIs at
the wafer scale into BAR, CROSS, or orthogonal states, validating
the method’s universality. The method also holds the potential
for resonance-wavelength correction of microring resonators.
Reduced spacing between deep trench rows is expected to yield
greater refractive index reduction and strengthen the trimming
effect. In addition to the lattice expansion and residual thermal
stress discussed in this work, potential effects such as stress
redistribution and cladding densification after annealing will be
explored in future studies to enrich the physical understanding.
Exploring strategies to increase the effective index would further
enhance the trimming flexibility. Overall, this post-fabrication
trimming technique offers a valuable solution to address fabri-
cation imperfections and enhance reliability of Si-PICs, enabling
next-generation energy-efficient and low-cost applications in
optical modulators, switches, and photonic computing.

6.1
Experimental Setup
For the optical path, light from a tunable laser (Santec TSL-550)
was first adjusted to TE polarization via a polarization controller,
then coupled into and out of the MZI chip through grating
couplers and finally detected by an optical power meter (OPM;
Yokogawa, AQ2211). For the electrical path, a precision voltage
source (PVS; Keysight B2901BL) applies the electrical signal to
the chip PADs using a probe. A computer program controls the
outputs of both the laser and PVS and records the readings of
OPM.
6.2
Calculation of Si Refractive Index Change
By tracking the trough points in P–T curves, heating power
difference (Δ𝑝𝑜𝑤𝑒𝑟) between pre- and post-trimming trough
positions can be obtained. Since the heating power in the
thermo-optic PS-WG is linearly proportional to the accumulated
optical phase shift, this Δ𝑝𝑜𝑤𝑒𝑟enables the calculation of the
corresponding thermo-optic phase offset Δ𝜑0 (Equation 1). Here,
Δ𝜑0 exactly compensates for the initial phase offset Δ𝜑induced
by high-temperature annealing; the two are equal in magnitude
but opposite in sign, as shown in Equation (2). Furthermore, the
change in the mode effective refractive index Δ𝑛𝑒𝑓𝑓induced by
trimming can be derived using Equation (3) [49].

Abstract: Limited by process precision for silicon photonic integrated circuits (Si-PICs), manufacturing deviations in waveguide width, etch depth, and layer thickness are inevitable. These variations cause initial phase shifts and compromise the performance of phase-sensitive devices such as Mach-Zehnder Interferometers (MZI) and microring resonators. To address this issue, we present a lossless, nonvolatile, and CMOS-compatible post-fabrication trimming method based on on-chip high-temperature annealing, assisted by highly thermally isolated undercut waveguides. The significant thermal stress during annealing exceeds the yield strength of silicon and induces microscopic modifications including irreversible lattice expansion verified by transmission electron microscopy, which ultimately reduces the mode effective refractive index. This novel approach requires no additional equipment beyond the standard CMOS fabrication and eliminates static power consumption after short-duration electrical stimulus. Trimming experiments on C- and O-band MZIs demonstrated a phase compensation over 4π, a tuning resolution over 6 bits, and stable operation beyond 8500 hours. Additionally, 15 randomly MZIs are precisely trimmed to BAR, CROSS, or orthogonal states, confirming the method’s universality. This practical technique enables reliable, scalable post-fabrication trimming for low-cost, energy-efficient Si-PIC applications such as optical modulating, switching, and computing.
